source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Teams of human national-security experts played a two-move US-China Taiwan Strait crisis wargame. Separate LLM-simulated teams played the same game. Humans and LLMs did not play each other. About half the 21 possible actions matched in frequency.
numbers: Humans: 214 experts in 48 teams. LLM arm: 10 teams of 6 simulated players x 8 treatment combinations = 80 games per configuration. Action frequency matched humans on 16 of 21 actions for GPT-3.5, 10 for GPT-4, 9 for GPT-4o. Bootstrap 95% CIs.
limits: One fictional scenario. Human and LLM games were separate, so no head-to-head test. Matching judged by action counts, not quality of reasoning.
agent_relevance: Simulated evaluation by LLM teams gives roughly the right high-level pattern but wrong details. Use as a rough screen, never as a verdict on a plan.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (treatment effects)
finding: Statistical conclusions on the scenario treatments (weapon accuracy, crew training, China posture) mostly agreed between LLM and human trials, but not for every model: GPT-4 and GPT-4o showed a crew-training effect that humans did not.
numbers: Treatments: AI weapon accuracy (no effect in humans or any LLM), crew training (no effect in humans; effect for GPT-4 and GPT-4o per Table 1), China posture (effect in humans and all LLMs).
limits: Only 3 treatments. Agreement on direction does not mean agreement on size. Table layout garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Check a simulator first on whether it moves the same way as humans when one scenario variable changes. Cheap validation for our simulate-a-plan step.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (dialog and aggressiveness)
finding: Simulating team dialog (instead of asking for the decision directly) made LLM teams more aggressive and closer to humans on aggressiveness, but they chose more actions in total, further from humans. Simulated dialog was short statements that rarely disagreed: farcical harmony.
numbers: Dialog length varied in chunks of about 350 words; final runs used about 1050 words per move (three chunks). Passive actions (hold fire at all costs, do not use the AI weapon) became less likely with longer dialog.
quote: This farcical harmony and the simulation results remain the same even when emphasized
limits: Effect depends on the LLM. Dialog improved with GPT-4 and GPT-4o over GPT-3.5 but stayed shallow.
agent_relevance: Multi-voice debate inside one model is not independent opposition (guardrail G4). Do not count simulated agreement as evidence.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (persona insensitivity)
finding: LLM simulations ignored player background. Describing all players as strict pacifists or aggressive sociopaths made no statistically significant difference in either move for any model.
numbers: No significant change for any action, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o, both moves. Adding the president's three priorities did change some action rates (GPT-3.5 raised Fire at Chinese vessels).
limits: One-line persona descriptions. Snow Globe (a11) found a persona effect in a different setup, so the null is not universal.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts may not give real diversity of opposition. Do not rely on them for red-team variety (schema section 4b).

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (consistency across moves)
finding: Humans and LLMs were both more aggressive in move 2 after aggressive move 1 actions. The drop after a de-escalatory move 1 was largest for GPT-4 and humans, and GPT-4 was closest to human behavior.
numbers: Conditional probabilities p(agg2|agg1) and p(agg2|des1) with bootstrap 95% CIs. Printed LLM values for p(agg2|agg1) range 0.94 to 1.00; p(agg2|des1) about 0.65 to 0.86. Human row layout garbled, so exact human values not recorded.
limits: Table text garbled in extraction; values approximate.
agent_relevance: LLM simulations are over-consistent. A simulated adversary may be too predictable compared with real people.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents (same model per run) played a turn-based diplomacy and war simulation over 14 days with 27 actions, from diplomatic visits to nuclear strike. All five models escalated, with sudden hard-to-predict spikes.
numbers: 10 simulations x 8 nations per model-scenario cell, three scenarios (neutral, invasion, cyberattack). Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.0, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base. A separate world-model LLM wrote consequences. Significant initial escalation for all models; none showed significant de-escalation.
limits: Scoring weights are the authors' own. Only 10 runs per cell. 2023-era models. The world model is itself an LLM adjudicator.
agent_relevance: If the simulated opponent and the adjudicator are both LLMs, test outcomes inherit model bias. Treat each outcome as one noisy draw.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (numbers by model)
finding: Escalation differed strongly by model. GPT-3.5 rose from escalation score 10.15 to 26.02 (256%) in the neutral scenario. The base model used nuclear actions far more than chat models.
numbers: Table 2 average escalation score by cell: GPT-4 about 9.8 to 11.8, GPT-3.5 about 17.8 to 21.9, Claude-2.0 3.4 to 6.7, Llama-2-Chat 4.4 to 5.8, GPT-4-Base 17.6 to 20.0. GPT-4-Base nuclear actions 6.7 to 7.1% of actions vs 0 to 0.21% for chat models. GPT-4-Base nuclear strikes 2.48 per nation vs 7.38 messages.
quote: A lot of countries have nuclear weapons. Some say they should disarm them, others like to posture. We have it! Let's use it.
limits: Table alignment partly garbled in extraction; values read from the printed table.
agent_relevance: Safety tuning changes simulated behavior a lot. Test the scaffold on the model it runs on.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (arms-race and reasoning)
finding: Agents built up military capacity steadily and justified escalation by deterrence and first-strike reasoning. Authors suspect agents equate more arms spending with more security.
numbers: Military capacity rose steadily over days in all models; rare nuclear outliers for GPT-3.5 and Llama-2-Chat in all scenarios.
limits: Reported chain-of-thought is not a faithful record of why an action was chosen.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a simulated agent's written justification as evidence of its cause (schema section 1).

source: Emery (2021) Moral Choices without Moral Language: 1950s Political-Military Wargaming at the RAND Corporation (Texas National Security Review 4(4))
finding: RAND ran two Cold War Games. The Mathematics Analysis Division version was formal and quantified; players went nuclear readily and opened with H-bomb exchanges. The Social Science Division version was free-play with area experts and never went nuclear.
numbers: MAD version 1954-55, two weeks, 19 countries, ended in atomic war in the final round. SSD version: 4 plays Feb 1955 to Apr 1956; round 4 had 13 team members. Pauly's MIT study: 26 games 1958-72, only 2 crossed the nuclear threshold; 64.9% of 77 participants reported extreme or intense emotional involvement.
quote: the U.S. and S.U. began with H-bombings as early moves
limits: Read via a fetch summary of the page (first 100000 of 112148 characters), not the PDF. The MAD game was a mathematical paper game, not a computer program; Rivera and Lamparth cite Emery for computer-assisted games leading to more nuclear use, a looser reading.
agent_relevance: Formalized, tabulated losses made nuclear use look cheap. A simulator that scores a plan by tabulated losses may under-count costs not in its model.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe is an LLM multi-agent system in which players, controller and adjudicator of a text wargame can each be AI or human. Authors argue LLMs for the first time allow automating qualitative (open-ended) wargames, which older automation (game theory, RAND RSAS expert systems, RL) could not.
numbers: Case 1: AI incident tabletop; a human group takes 20 minutes or more, the simulation runs in under one minute on a consumer GPU. Case 2: geopolitical crisis, each of 3 persona combinations run 20 times with one one-year move.
limits: Descriptive paper, no human validation of realism. Authors say not to trust the raw probabilities.
agent_relevance: A cheap open-ended simulation can be run many times to see a spread of outcomes. Fits the test-by-running state if the spread is reported, not one run.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Snow Globe: persona case study
finding: Armed conflict frequency rose with hawk personas. This contrasts with the null persona result of Lamparth et al. on a different game.
numbers: Armed conflict in 20 runs: dove-dove 1/20, dove-hawk 4/20, hawk-hawk 14/20.
limits: Tiny N, one scenario, authors' own scenario text, no replication. Personas stated concrete goals (start a war if needed), unlike background descriptions.
agent_relevance: Persona instructions that state concrete goals change outcomes; vague background does not. Give adversary roles explicit goals and constraints.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Snow Globe: hallucination as feature
finding: Authors argue hallucination is useful in adjudication because plausible invention of consequences is the point. Common low-quality failures: repeated output from move to move, and output that deviates from players' stated plans. Adding the three words 'Include unexpected consequences' changed adjudication.
numbers: Qualitative; no failure counts given.
quote: Hallucination, which in other applications is so often harmful, is the key to making open-ended LLM wargames work.
limits: Opinion plus anecdote. Conflicts with grounded adjudication in our schema (G3, G8).
agent_relevance: Check the adjudicator in code: does the outcome follow from the stated move? Drift from the plan is the known failure.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformers for Accelerated Course of Action Development in Military Operations
finding: An LLM generates courses of action from mission text (and optionally an image); a commander can give feedback. COAs are scored by running them in a militarized StarCraft II scenario (TigerClaw). This is simulated evaluation of plans by actually running them.
numbers: 5 COAs per variant x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts per variant. Human expert 15 trials. COA-GPT without feedback beat all AI baselines on mean total reward, including Autocurriculum RL; the best vision-plus-feedback variant scored 3.4% below the human expert. Autocurriculum RL needed 112 thousand simulated battles (70 million timesteps, 35 workers). COA-GPT makes COAs in seconds.
limits: One scenario, one game. RL baseline numbers copied from earlier work, not rerun. COA-GPT had higher friendly casualties than baselines (one command at the start, low control resolution). The human expert had lowest friendly and highest hostile casualties. Game is mostly deterministic, so variance comes from COA diversity.
agent_relevance: Generate then run: plan quality read from a simulator score, not from model opinion. Human feedback rounds raised mean reward and cut variance. Fits our check-by-running loop.

source: Shrivastava, Hullman and Lamparth (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Free-form crisis answers from five LMs were semantically inconsistent across 20 samples, measured as 1 minus rescaled BERTScore F1. Inconsistency stayed high when countries were anonymized or temperature changed. Semantically equivalent prompt rewording could cause more inconsistency than temperature sampling.
numbers: 20 responses per setting at T=1.05 (T=1.0 in some experiments), all unique pairs. Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini. Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini least inconsistent, GPT-4 most. Validation ablations: lexical 0.08, syntactic 0.17, semantic shift 0.37; scores of 0.25 or more treated as semantic variation. Example GPT-4 pair scored 0.73. Any temperature of 0.2 or more exceeds inconsistency from semantic-preserving rewording.
limits: BERTScore similarity is an indirect measure of meaning. Prompt-sensitivity effects measured at T=0.
agent_relevance: One sample from an LLM simulator is not a stable answer. Report spread over samples and reword prompts to test stability (G4, repeated-run checks).

source: Shrivastava et al. (2024) continuation result
finding: Adding wargame continuations (later moves) lowered inconsistency versus the initial setting for each model. The revisionist continuation gave the lowest inconsistency.
numbers: Inconsistency decreased for every model with continuations; no individual pair of responses was semantically consistent across all settings and models.
limits: Per-model values were in figures, not read numerically.
agent_relevance: Committing to a trajectory lowers variance, so the early plan choice drives simulation variance.

source: Hua et al. (2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based Multi-Agent Simulation of World Wars
finding: Country agents simulate WWI, WWII and the Warring States period. Results are scored against historical records on alliances, war declarations and mobilization (Jaccard similarity). Counterfactual trigger events test which triggers cause war.
numbers: Seven runs per setting, evaluated at round 6. Default setting: over 75% accuracy on alliances and over 90% on mobilization; war declaration accuracy low (about 18% or less in the printed table). A world war broke out in all simulations without exception. De-anonymized WWI: alliance 97.43% for all three models, mobilization 100%, war declaration 13 to 19%.
limits: Claude-2 and GPT-3.5 formed senseless alliances (could not apply enemy-of-an-enemy logic). Table text partly garbled. Recall of training-data history is a confound.
agent_relevance: Knowing history is not simulating. Test fidelity against known outcomes and use counterfactual checks to see whether the model reasons or recalls.

source: Hua et al. (2024) WarAgent counterfactual knowledge injection
finding: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 on a peaceful WWI counterfactual still produced a world war in simulation. Authors read this as the simulation not relying only on memorized history.
numbers: 7 runs after fine-tuning (3 epochs). Accuracy dropped on some aspects (e.g., 43.38 vs 31.02 and 78.06 vs 62.12; column labels garbled). World war still broke out.
limits: War broke out in every setting, which also suggests a strong built-in bias toward war, not proof of reasoning. Fine-tuning also degraded reasoning.
agent_relevance: An outcome that does not move when facts are changed is a warning sign: a simulator that always ends the same way cannot tell plans apart.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames (scoping review)
finding: Scoping review of 223 de-duplicated AI-in-wargames papers (to 1 May 2026) coded by whether the LM has open-ended control over player actions, adjudication, or both. Only 20 of 223 (9%) give LMs both roles.
numbers: 20 of 223 (9%) both-creative; 17 of 223 (7.6%) under a stricter filter; 4 of 63 (6.3%) core military-wargame papers. 155 of 223 (70%) engage at least one safety theme. 20 of 22 RL-coded studies and all 3 symbolic studies are in the rigid rule-based quadrant; none in both-creative.
limits: Authors' own rubric and catalog. A review, not an effect measurement.
agent_relevance: Little evidence exists on LLM adjudication validity. Do not assume an LLM judge of plan outcomes is valid; prefer rule-based or code adjudication where possible.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) quadrant framework for AI wargames
finding: Four-way classification by player creativity and adjudicator creativity. Q-I: rule-based both (chess, Go, StarCraft, original Kriegspiel). Q-IV: both open-ended (real serious wargames). Language-rich but rule-resolved games such as many Diplomacy evaluations sit in Q-III.
numbers: Q-I to Q-IV defined by LOW/HIGH player and adjudicator creativity; RL and search methods thrive where rules are rigid.
limits: Taxonomy is the authors' own and its reliability is untested.
agent_relevance: Choose the quadrant on purpose: code adjudication for checkable parts, LLM adjudication only for open-ended parts, flagged as unvalidated.

source: Black and Darken (2023) Scaling Intelligent Agents in Combat Simulations for Wargaming (I/ITSEC)
finding: Hierarchical RL agents for combat simulation. A multi-model framework (several state abstractions) beat the best single model by 62.6%. More models beat fewer models even when the added ones were worse abstractions.
numbers: Preliminary test over 1,000 games, 10x10 board, 2 to 4 agents per side, 30 phases, 2 million steps. Mean score: scripted baseline 813.750 (sd 6.253), RL-global 1095.601 (sd 62.972), RL-local 7x7 1070.512 (sd 24.992).
limits: Preliminary, one scenario, toy board. Authors say no AI has yet reached human level in long-horizon combat modeling.
agent_relevance: Different state abstractions give diverse cheap evaluators. This resembles a mixed-view check only if the views really differ, unlike same-model samples.

source: Black (2024) Mastering the Digital Art of War: Intelligent Combat Simulation Agents for Wargaming Using Hierarchical RL (NPS thesis)
finding: Thesis behind the scaling paper: HRL framework, multi-model decision framework, dimension-invariant observation abstractions, intrinsic rewards for long-term planning.
numbers: Only the cover page was read; no numbers taken.
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Pointer to the RL branch of automated wargaming.

source: Meta FAIR et al. (2022) Human-level play in the game of Diplomacy by combining language models with strategic reasoning (CICERO)
finding: CICERO pairs a language model with a planning engine to play full-press Diplomacy. Lamparth et al. cite it as the example of language plus strategic planning reaching human-level play.
numbers: Not opened: Science page returned 403 and the search budget ran out. No figures recorded.
limits: Known only from citation text in opened papers.
agent_relevance: Planning stays in a search engine while the language model handles talk. Matches our rule that code decides and the model fills slots.

source: Bakhtin et al. (2022) Mastering the Game of No-Press Diplomacy via Human-Regularized Reinforcement Learning and Planning (DiL-piKL, Diplodocus)
finding: Self-play RL alone is not enough for games needing cooperation with humans. DiL-piKL pulls a reward-maximizing policy toward a human-imitation policy.
numbers: Abstract only: 200-game tournament with 62 human players; two Diplodocus agents outscored every participant who played more than two games and ranked first and third on Elo.
limits: Abstract seen through a fetch summary only. No-press (no language) variant.
agent_relevance: A simulated opponent regularized toward human play is more realistic than one trained only against itself. Relevant for modelling adversaries.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) discussion of the computer-automation claim
finding: Authors repeat that early US military efforts to replace humans with computer models led to more rational play but more nuclear use (Emery 2021), then test LLM teams and find broad agreement with humans but specific shifts.
numbers: LLM arm used GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o; GPT-4 closest to humans on conditional behavior.
limits: Emery's paper (a09) describes a mathematical game run by a RAND division, not a computer program.
agent_relevance: Do not cite computers cause nuclear use as hard evidence. The base source is a historical case study of a few plays.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) design and limits
finding: Models were not told they were in a simulation. Authors say prompt details likely affect behavior and call for more analysis before deployment.
numbers: Fixed 10 runs per cell; 14 simulated days; 27 actions in six severity categories (de-escalation, status quo, posturing, non-violent escalation, violent escalation, nuclear).
limits: Confidence intervals bootstrap over 10 runs of 8 nations, but nations in one run share a model and world state, so they are not independent.
agent_relevance: Report independence honestly: agents inside one run are correlated.

source: Cranfield and AIAA studies named in SUBFIELDS.md
finding: The SUBFIELDS row cites Cranfield and AIAA studies from search results only. I found no paper by that name in the arXiv searches, so I did not use it. The opened evidence base is LLM-era (2023-2026) work plus RAND history.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Unverified. The row's key-work label looks unreliable.
agent_relevance: Treat the evidence base for automated wargaming as thin: few controlled studies, mostly 2024 LLM papers with small N.
